core: What advertising is: the working definition — any paid form of nonpersonal communication about a product, service, or idea from an identified sponsor (attributed to the AMA Universal Marketing Dictionary and OpenStax Principles of Marketing / Introduction to Business)
The major media: television, print (newspapers and magazines), digital (internet and mobile), outdoor (billboards and transit) — one line and one original example each
Advertising in the promotion mix: paid media versus owned and earned media; public relations and content marketing named as sibling topics
The objectives: inform, persuade, remind — one line each
Targeting: ads aimed at chosen audiences; market segmentation named as a sibling topic (reference only)
Truth in advertising: FTC requirement that claims be truthful, not deceptive or unfair, and substantiated; ethics in marketing named as a sibling topic
The honest framing: advertising buys attention, not trust
supporting: Advertising as one element of the promotional mix alongside personal selling, sales promotion, public relations, social media, and e-commerce
Message and media decisions as part of an advertising plan (right message, right time, right audience)
The FTC's role in enforcing truth-in-advertising rules
outOfScope: The promotion mix and promotion strategy as a whole (sibling topic marketing:foundations:promotion)
Digital advertising mechanics — targeting platforms, auction models, measurement (sibling topic marketing:foundations:digital-advertising)
Social media marketing platforms and practices (sibling topic marketing:foundations:social-media-marketing)
Ethics in marketing beyond the factual FTC line (sibling topic marketing:foundations:ethics-in-marketing)

claims.claim: Advertising is any paid form of nonpersonal communication about a product, service, or idea from an identified sponsor, delivered through media channels to reach many recipients at once.
Advertising is one element of the promotion mix; the promotional mix also includes personal selling, sales promotion, public relations, social media, and e-commerce.

Advertising is paid media: the sponsor rents time or space and therefore controls the message, unlike earned coverage (public relations) or owned channels (the organization's own website, blog, or social accounts).
The traditional advertising media include newspapers and magazines (print), television, radio, the internet and mobile devices (digital), and billboards (outdoor).

Common advertising objectives are to inform (build awareness, especially for new products), to persuade (convince consumers by highlighting benefits), and to remind (keep an established product in the customer's mind).
Advertisers aim messages at a chosen target audience, selecting media and crafting the message to reach that group.
Under U.S. law, claims in advertisements must be truthful, cannot be deceptive or unfair, and must be evidence-based; the Federal Trade Commission enforces these consumer-protection rules.
Advertising buys attention, not trust: an ad can put a message in front of a large audience, but belief depends on the advertiser's record and the support behind its claims.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The wording of the working definition differs slightly across authoritative sources: the AMA Universal Marketing Dictionary emphasizes nonpersonal, paid announcements that inform or persuade a target market (alternative form: nonpersonal communication conducted through paid media by a sponsor identifiable by the audience); OpenStax Introduction to Business 12.5 says 'any paid form of nonpersonal promotion by an identified sponsor delivered through traditional media channels'; OpenStax Principles of Marketing 14.1 says 'paid communication messages that identify a brand or organization... intended to reach a large number of recipients.'
positions: AMA dictionary: nonpersonal, paid announcements; inform or persuade a target market; sponsor identifiable by the audience
OpenStax Introduction to Business 12.5: paid form of nonpersonal promotion by an identified sponsor, delivered through traditional media channels
OpenStax Principles of Marketing 14.1: paid communication messages that identify a brand or organization, intended to reach a large number of recipients
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the classic combined working definition (paid + nonpersonal + identified sponsor + about a product, service, or idea) as a synthesis attributed to the AMA marketing dictionary and the two OpenStax texts; all three sources agree on the three defining elements, so the synthesis is faithful and the minor wording differences are noted here rather than hidden.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft's boilerplate opener ('Advertising is a foundational concept in Marketing. This lesson introduces its meaning...') carries no verifiable content and was replaced entirely with source-verified material.
The draft objective 'Define advertising using course-appropriate language' was replaced with the attributed working definition and concrete, checkable objectives.
The draft contained no practice questions; a five-question bank was written from the researched material.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic draft with a source-verified lesson anchored to the AMA Universal Marketing Dictionary (marketing-dictionary.org), OpenStax Principles of Marketing 14.1-14.2, and OpenStax Introduction to Business 12.5, with the FTC line from the FTC's Advertising and Marketing guidance.
Attributed the working definition and documented the minor wording differences among sources in conflictingEvidence.
Kept promotion, public relations, content marketing, digital advertising, social media marketing, market segmentation, and ethics in marketing as sibling references only, per the topic brief.
Wrote five original scenario questions with spread answer keys (A:2, B:1, C:1, D:1) and both recall and application/analysis items.
All ad examples are original and fictional (Gable Street Roasters, Riverside Cycles, Bluebird Bakery, Meadow Bakery, Harbor Books, Rosa's bakery).

sourceRecords.title: Advertising and Marketing (business guidance)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Registry record reused with identical URL; read live via curl on 2026-08-22. States that under the law, claims in advertisements must be truthful, cannot be deceptive or unfair, and must be evidence-based. Supports the truth-in-advertising claim and the attention-not-trust framing. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: About the FTC
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Registry record reused with identical URL. States the FTC enforces federal consumer protection laws that prevent deceptive and unfair business practices; supports the one-line statement that the FTC enforces truth-in-advertising rules.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, Section 12.5: Promotion Strategy
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Registry record reused with identical URL; read via a Wayback Machine capture of the canonical section URL on 2026-08-22. Defines traditional advertising as any paid form of nonpersonal promotion by an identified sponsor delivered through traditional media channels, and lists the elements of the promotional mix (advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations, social media, e-commerce). Definitions paraphrased with attribution; the identified-sponsor clause of the working definition rests on this source.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, Section 14.1: Advertising in the Promotion Mix
sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Dr. Maria Gomez Albrecht, Dr. Mark Green, Linda Hoffman)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. New record; openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so the canonical section URL was read via a Wayback Machine capture (web.archive.org/web/2025/...) on 2026-08-22. Defines advertising as paid communication messages that identify a brand or organization and are intended to reach a large number of recipients; names newspapers, magazines, television, radio, Internet, and billboards as traditional media and adds mobile, email, and social media; discusses awareness, reminders, and audiences' reluctance to believe ads (support for the attention-not-trust framing).

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, Section 14.2: Major Decisions in Developing an Advertising Plan
sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Dr. Maria Gomez Albrecht, Dr. Mark Green, Linda Hoffman)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. New record; read via a Wayback Machine capture of the canonical section URL on 2026-08-22. States that common advertising objectives include information, persuasion, comparisons, and reminders, and defines informative, persuasive, and reminder advertising; describes the advertising plan's decisions (objectives, strategy, budget, execution, assessment) and sending the right message at the right time to the right audience; discusses the target audience in message creation.

sourceRecords.title: Advertising (Universal Marketing Dictionary)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A dictionary source (online home of the former AMA Dictionary of Marketing Terms), read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Defines advertising as the promotional method involving the placement and use of nonpersonal, paid announcements and messages in time or space, with advertisers seeking to inform or persuade members of a particular target market regarding their goods, services, organizations, or ideas; alternative definition: nonpersonal communication conducted through paid media by a sponsor identifiable by the audience. Definitions paraphrased with attribution; supports the working definition, the paid-media point, the objectives, and targeting.
